## Ball Bearings and Bushings {#chap-08-bearings} ### Learning Objectives {#sec-objectives-08} By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. **Classify** bearing types by their operating principles and load capabilities 2. **Select** appropriate ball bearing types for different applications 3. **Calculate** bearing life (L10) using the basic rating life equation 4. **Apply** load factors to determine equivalent dynamic bearing loads 5. **Determine** required dynamic load ratings for specified life requirements 6. **Explain** the hydrodynamic wedge effect and how a rotating shaft floats on an oil cushion 7. **Interpret** the Stribeck curve and identify the three lubrication regimes (boundary, mixed, hydrodynamic) 8. **Connect** bushing performance to sintered bearing manufacturing (see Chapter @sec-chap-sintering) ::: {.callout-think} **Before You Read:** Every rotating machine—from tiny precision instruments to massive industrial equipment—relies on bearings. What functions do you think bearings serve, and why can't rotating shafts simply rest directly in their housings? ::: ### Introduction to Bearings {#sec-bearings-intro} Bearings are machine elements that **constrain relative motion** and **reduce friction** between moving parts. They are fundamental to virtually every rotating machine—from tiny precision instruments to massive industrial equipment. Bearings serve three primary functions: 1. **Support loads** (radial and/or thrust) 2. **Reduce friction** between moving surfaces 3. **Guide motion** with precision and repeatability --- #### Classification of Bearings {-} Bearings are broadly classified into two main categories: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Classification of bearing types.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/bearing-classification-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: --- ### Ball Bearings {-} Ball bearings are the most common type of rolling element bearing. They use spherical balls as the rolling elements, held between an inner race and an outer race. #### Anatomy of a Ball Bearing {-} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cross-section of a deep groove ball bearing showing main components.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/ball-bearing-anatomy-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: **Key Components:** | Component | Function | |:----------|:---------| | **Inner Race** | Mounted on the shaft; rotates with the shaft | | **Outer Race** | Mounted in the housing; typically stationary | | **Rolling Elements** | Balls that roll between races, carrying the load | | **Cage (Retainer)** | Separates and guides the balls to prevent contact | | **Seals/Shields** | Keep lubricant in and contaminants out | --- #### Types of Ball Bearings {-} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Common Ball Bearing Types and Applications
Type Load Capacity Typical Applications Key Feature
Deep Groove Radial + light axial Electric motors, pumps, gearboxes Most versatile; handles combined loads
Angular Contact Combined radial + high axial Machine tool spindles, pumps Contact angle 15-40 deg; paired for bidirectional thrust
Self-Aligning Radial + light axial Conveyors, fans, textile machinery Tolerates shaft deflection and misalignment
Thrust Ball Axial only Automotive steering, crane hooks 90 deg contact angle; cannot handle radial loads
````` ::: ::: --- ### Ball Bearing Life Calculations {#bearing-life} The life of a rolling element bearing is inherently **statistical**—even identical bearings operating under identical conditions will fail at different times due to the random nature of material fatigue. Understanding this statistical behavior is essential for proper bearing selection and reliability engineering. #### Understanding Statistical Bearing Life {-} ::: {.callout-think} **Before You Read:** If you tested 100 identical bearings under identical loads and speeds, would they all fail at the same time? What factors might cause variation in their lifetimes? ::: When bearings fail, they do so by **fatigue spalling**—small flakes of material breaking away from the rolling surfaces due to repeated stress cycles. The location where a fatigue crack initiates depends on microscopic material imperfections (inclusions, voids, grain boundaries) that vary randomly from bearing to bearing, even in high-quality manufacturing. If we test a large group of identical bearings under identical conditions and plot the number of failures against operating time, we get a distribution of bearing lives. This distribution is **not** a normal (Gaussian) distribution—it follows a **Weibull distribution**, which is skewed to the right. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Statistical distribution of bearing failures showing L10, L50, and mean life concepts.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/bearing-life-distribution-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: #### L10 vs. L50: Which Life Do We Use? {-} The figure above illustrates several important life values: | Life Designation | Definition | Typical Relationship | |:-----------------|:-----------|:---------------------| | **L10** | Life exceeded by 90% of bearings | **Design basis** (conservative) | | **L50** (median) | Life exceeded by 50% of bearings | L50 ≈ 5 × L10 | | **Mean life** | Average life of all bearings | Mean ≈ 5.4 × L10 | ::: {.callout-industry} **Why L10, not L50?** In most engineering applications, we design for the **L10 life** because: 1. **Safety margin:** 90% of bearings will exceed this life—conservative design 2. **Replacement planning:** We know when 10% might start failing 3. **Industry standard:** All bearing catalogs use L10 ratings (ISO 281) If we designed for L50 life, half of our bearings would fail before the "rated" life—unacceptable for most applications! ::: The relationship between L10 and L50 also explains an important insight: if a bearing achieves its L10 life, it still has substantial remaining life. The **median bearing** (L50) lasts about 5 times longer than L10! #### The L10 Life Concept {-} > **Definition:** The L10 life is the number of revolutions (or hours at a given speed) that **90% of a group of identical bearings** will complete or exceed before the first evidence of fatigue failure (flaking/spalling). In other words, 10% of bearings will fail before reaching L10 life, while 90% will survive. #### Basic Life Equation {-} The fundamental bearing life equation is: $$L_{10} = \left(\frac{C}{P}\right)^p \times 10^6 \text{ revolutions}$$ **Where:** | Symbol | Description | Units | |:-------|:------------|:------| | $L_{10}$ | Basic rating life | revolutions | | $C$ | Basic dynamic load rating | N or lbf | | $P$ | Equivalent dynamic bearing load | N or lbf | | $p$ | Life exponent | — | **Life Exponent Values:** - **Ball bearings:** $p = 3$ - **Roller bearings:** $p = 10/3 \approx 3.33$ #### Converting to Hours {-} For bearings operating at constant speed, it is more practical to express life in hours: $$L_{10h} = \frac{L_{10}}{60 \cdot n} = \frac{1}{60 \cdot n}\left(\frac{C}{P}\right)^p \times 10^6 \text{ hours}$$ Where $n$ is the rotational speed in RPM. This simplifies to: $$L_{10h} = \frac{10^6}{60 \cdot n}\left(\frac{C}{P}\right)^p$$ --- #### Equivalent Dynamic Load {-} When a bearing experiences both radial ($F_r$) and axial ($F_a$) loads simultaneously, an **equivalent dynamic load** ($P$) must be calculated: $$P = X \cdot F_r + Y \cdot F_a$$ **Where:** | Factor | Description | |:-------|:------------| | $X$ | Radial load factor (from bearing tables) | | $Y$ | Axial load factor (from bearing tables) | | $F_r$ | Applied radial load | | $F_a$ | Applied axial (thrust) load | For **pure radial loading** (most common case): $P = F_r$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

It represents: > The constant radial load that a bearing can theoretically endure for a basic rating life of **one million revolutions**. Typical catalog format: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

The basic dynamic load rating for radial ball bearings is determined by: $$C = f_c \cdot (i \cdot \cos\alpha)^{0.7} \cdot Z^{2/3} \cdot D^{1.8}$$ **Where:** | Symbol | Description | Units | |:-------|:------------|:------| | $C$ | Basic dynamic load rating | N (metric) or lbf (inch) | | $f_c$ | Geometry and material factor | — (from table) | | $i$ | Number of rows of balls | — | | $\alpha$ | Contact angle | degrees | | $Z$ | Number of balls per row | — | | $D$ | Ball diameter | mm (metric) or inches (inch) | The factor $f_c$ depends on the bearing geometry and is tabulated based on the ratio $\frac{D \cos\alpha}{d_m}$, where $d_m$ is the pitch diameter of the ball set. ::: {.callout-think} **Consider This:** Looking at the formula, which parameter has the greatest influence on load capacity? The ball diameter $D$ appears with an exponent of 1.8—nearly squared! This means **doubling the ball diameter increases load capacity by a factor of** $2^{1.8} \approx 3.5$. ::: ##### Values of $f_c$ (Geometry Factor) {-} The following table provides $f_c$ values based on the bearing geometry ratio. Use the **Metric** column when ball diameter $D$ is in mm (result is $C$ in Newtons). This has profound practical implications: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Effect of Load Changes on Bearing Life (Cubic Relationship)
Change Load Ratio Effect on Life
Double the load P → 2P L₁₀ → L₁₀/8 (life reduced to 1/8)
Halve the load P → P/2 L₁₀ → 8×L₁₀ (life increased 8×)
Reduce load by 20% P → 0.8P L₁₀ → 1.95×L₁₀ (life nearly doubles)
Increase load by 20% P → 1.2P L₁₀ → 0.58×L₁₀ (life nearly halves)
````` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-industry} **Design Insight:** If you can reduce the bearing load by just 20%, you nearly **double** the bearing life! Conversely, underestimating loads by 20% will cut your bearing life nearly in half. This is why accurate load analysis is critical in bearing selection. In automotive applications, this relationship explains why bearing failures often cluster around vehicles that operate at higher loads (towing, heavy cargo) even when the bearings are "the same" as those in lightly-loaded vehicles. ::: ::: {.callout-check} **Quick Check:** A bearing is rated for C = 10,000 N and operates at P = 2,500 N, giving L₁₀ = 64 million revolutions. If the load is reduced to P = 1,250 N (half), what is the new L₁₀ life? *Answer: L₁₀ = (10,000/1,250)³ × 10⁶ = 8³ × 10⁶ = **512 million revolutions** (8× longer!)* ::: --- #### How Much Life is Required? {-} Before selecting a bearing, engineers must determine the **required design life** for the application. The table below provides industry guidelines for different machine types: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Type of Machine Examples Life (hours)
Instruments and apparatus used infrequently Demonstration apparatus, devices for operation of sliding doors 500
Aircraft engines — 500–2,000
Machines for short duration or intermittent operation (service interruptions minor) Hand tools, lifting tackle in machinery shops, hand-driven machines, farm machinery, assembly cranes, charging machines, foundry cranes, household machines 4,000–8,000
Machines for intermittent service where dependable operation is important Auxiliary machines in power stations, conveying equipment in production lines, elevators, general-cargo cranes, machine tools used less frequently 8,000–12,000
Machines for 8-hour service not always fully utilized Machines in general mechanical industries, cranes for continuous service, blowers, jackshafts 20,000–30,000
Machines for continuous operation (24-hour service) Separators, compressors, pumps, mainline shafting, roller beds and conveyor rollers, mine hoists, stationary electric motors 40,000–60,000
Machines for 24-hour service where dependability is critical Pulp and paper machines, public power stations, mine pumps, public pumping stations, machines for continuous service aboard ships 100,000–200,000
````` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-industry} **Design Tip:** When in doubt, design for longer life. A bearing that costs 20% more but lasts twice as long often reduces total cost of ownership significantly—especially when considering downtime and labor costs for replacement. ::: --- #### Two Approaches to Bearing Selection {-} There are two common scenarios when working with bearing life equations: **Scenario A: Verify a Known Bearing** — You have a specific bearing (dimensions known) and want to check if it meets application requirements. **Scenario B: Select a Bearing** — You know the application requirements (load, speed, life) and need to find a bearing that meets them. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Two Approaches to Bearing Selection
Scenario What You Know What to Calculate When to Use
A: Verify existing bearing Bearing dimensions (Z, D, dm), or catalog C value C from dimensions, then L₁₀ Checking if a bearing in a machine meets requirements; validating catalog data
B: Select new bearing Required life (L), speed (n), load (P) Required C, then select from catalog Designing a new machine; replacing a failed bearing with adequate life
````` ::: ::: The following examples demonstrate both approaches. --- #### Applied Example: Calculate C from Bearing Dimensions {#example-calc-C-dimensions} ::: {.question} Find the basic dynamic load rating $C$ for a **207 radial bearing** with contact angle $\alpha = 0°$. From Table @tbl-conrad-bearing-table, the 207 bearing has: - Bore: 35 mm (1.378 in) - Outside diameter: 72 mm (2.8346 in) - Number of balls: Z = 9 - Ball diameter: D = 7/16 in = 0.4375 in ::: ::: {.answer} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Calculating C from Bearing Dimensions (207 Bearing)
Step Formula Calculation Result
Step 1: Pitch diameter dm = (OD + bore) / 2 dm = (2.8346 + 1.378) / 2 2.1063 in
Step 2: Geometry ratio (D·cos α) / dm (0.4375 × 1) / 2.1063 0.208
Step 3: Look up fc From Table (ratio ≈ 0.208) Interpolate between 0.20 and 0.22 fc = 4550
Step 4: Row-angle term (i·cos α)^0.7 (1 × 1)^0.7 1
Step 5: Ball count term Z^(2/3) 9^(2/3) 4.327
Step 6: Ball diameter term D^1.8 0.4375^1.8 0.2258
Step 7: Dynamic load rating C = fc × (i·cos α)^0.7 × Z^(2/3) × D^1.8 4550 × 1 × 4.327 × 0.2258 4446 lbf
````` ::: ::: ###### Verification {-} $$C = f_c \cdot (i \cos\alpha)^{0.7} \cdot Z^{2/3} \cdot D^{1.8} = 4550 \times 1 \times 9^{2/3} \times 0.4375^{1.8} = \boxed{4440\ \text{lbf}}$$ This matches the catalog value of **C = 4,440 lbf** from Table @tbl-conrad-bearing-table, confirming our calculation. ::: --- #### Applied Example: Calculate Allowable Load P {#example-calc-P} ::: {.question} For the **207 bearing** where we found C = 4,440 lbf, find the maximum radial load $P$ for a required L₁₀ life of **500 hours** at **1,500 RPM**. ::: ::: {.answer} We need to rearrange the life equation to solve for P: $$L_{10h} = \frac{10^6}{60 \cdot n}\left(\frac{C}{P}\right)^3$$ Solving for P: $$P = \sqrt[3]{\frac{10^6 \cdot C^3}{60 \cdot n \cdot L_{10h}}}$$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Calculating Maximum Load P for Required Life
Step Formula Calculation Result
Given C, L₁₀h, n C = 4440 lbf, L = 500 hrs, n = 1500 rpm —
Rearranged formula P = ∛(10⁶·C³ / 60·n·L) Solve life equation for P —
Numerator 10⁶ × C³ 10⁶ × 4440³ = 8.75e+16 8.753e+16
Denominator 60 × n × L 60 × 1500 × 500 45 000 000
Division Num / Denom 8.75e+16 / 45 000 000 1.945e+09
Cube root P = ∛(result) ∛(1.95e+09) 1248 lbf
````` ::: ::: ###### Conclusion {-} $$P = \sqrt[3]{\frac{10^6 \times 4440^3}{60 \times 1500 \times 500}} = \sqrt[3]{1.945 \times 10^9} = \boxed{1250\ \text{lbf}}$$ **Interpretation:** This bearing can support a radial load of **1,250 lbf** in an application where 90% of bearings will last at least 500 hours at 1,500 RPM. ::: --- #### Applied Example: Select a Bearing for Required Life {#example-select-bearing} ::: {.question} A bearing of the **X07 family** (35 mm bore) needs to run for **2,000 hours** at **5,000 RPM** and carry a load of **415 lbf**. Which bearing from the X07 family should be selected? ::: ::: {.answer} We need to find the **required** dynamic load rating C, then select a bearing that meets or exceeds this value. Rearranging the life equation to solve for C: $$C = \sqrt[3]{\frac{60 \cdot n \cdot L_{10h} \cdot P^3}{10^6}}$$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Calculating Required C for Bearing Selection
Step Formula Calculation Result
Given L, n, P L = 2000 hrs, n = 5000 rpm, P = 415 lbf —
Rearranged formula C = ∛(60·n·L·P³ / 10⁶) Solve life equation for C —
Numerator 60 × n × L × P³ 60 × 5000 × 2000 × 415³ 4.288e+16
Division Num / 10⁶ 4.29e+16 / 10⁶ 4.288e+10
Cube root C_required = ∛(result) ∛(4.29e+10) 3500 lbf
````` ::: ::: ###### Bearing Selection {-} $$C_{required} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{60 \times 5000 \times 2000 \times 415^3}{10^6}} = \sqrt[3]{4.29 \times 10^{10}} = \boxed{3500\ \text{lbf}}$$ Now compare with available X07 family bearings from Table @tbl-conrad-bearing-table: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

207 4440 Yes (4440 > 3500) ✓
307 5750 Yes (5750 > 3500)
````` ::: ::: ###### Conclusion {-} Select the **207 bearing** (C = 4,440 lbf). It exceeds the required C of 3,500 lbf while being more compact and economical than the 307. The 107 bearing is **not suitable**—its C = 2,760 lbf is below the required 3,500 lbf, meaning it would fail before reaching the design life. ::: {.callout-check} **Why not choose the 307?** While the 307 would work (C = 5,750 lbf), it's physically larger and more expensive. The 207 provides adequate life with a safety margin of 4,440/3,500 = 1.27, which is acceptable for most applications. ::: ::: --- #### Adjusted Rating Life {-} The basic L10 equation assumes ideal operating conditions. In practice, factors such as **reliability requirements**, **lubrication quality**, and **contamination** affect bearing life. The **adjusted rating life** accounts for these factors: $$L_{na} = a_1 \cdot a_2 \cdot a_3 \cdot L_{10}$$ Or using the modern ISO 281 formulation: $$L_{nm} = a_1 \cdot a_{ISO} \cdot L_{10}$$ **Where:** | Factor | Description | Typical Values | |:-------|:------------|:---------------| | $a_1$ | Life adjustment factor for reliability | See table below | | $a_2$ | Material factor | 0.5 to 2.0 (modern steels ≈ 1.0) | | $a_3$ | Operating conditions factor | 0.1 to 1.0 | | $a_{ISO}$ | Combined lubrication-contamination factor | 0.1 to 50 | **Reliability Factor ($a_1$):** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Reliability Factor a₁
Reliability Life Symbol a₁
90% L10 1.00
95% L5 0.64
96% L4 0.55
97% L3 0.47
98% L2 0.37
99% L1 0.25
````` ::: ::: --- #### Life Calculation Plot {-} The following plot illustrates how bearing life varies with the C/P ratio: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bearing life as a function of load ratio (C/P).](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/bearing-life-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: > **Design Insight:** A small increase in bearing size (higher C) or reduction in load (lower P) dramatically increases bearing life due to the cubic relationship. --- ### Applied Example: Ball Bearing Life Calculation {#bearing-example} ::: {.question} A deep groove ball bearing (6207) supports a shaft rotating at **1,750 RPM**. The bearing experiences a **radial load of 3,500 N** and an **axial load of 800 N**. Determine: 1. The equivalent dynamic load ($P$) 2. The basic L10 life in hours 3. The L5 life (95% reliability) in hours **Given data from catalog:** - Bearing: 6207 - Dynamic load rating: $C = 26.0$ kN = 26,000 N - For Fa/Fr ratio, use: $e = 0.24$, $X = 0.56$, $Y = 1.6$ ::: --- ::: {.answer} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Ball Bearing Life Calculation Steps
Step Calculation Result
Step 1: Check load ratio Fa/Fr = 800 / 3500 = 0.229 ≤ e: Use X=1, Y=0
Step 2: Equivalent load (P) P = X·Fr + Y·Fa = 0.56×3500 + 1.6×800 3500 N
Step 3: L10 (revolutions) L10 = (C/P)³ × 10⁶ = (26/3.5)³ × 10⁶ 409.9 million rev
Step 4: L10 (hours) L10h = L10 / (60 × n) = 409.9×10⁶ / (60 × 1750) 3 904 hours
Step 5: L5 (95% reliability) L5 = a₁ × L10 = 0.64 × 3904 2 499 hours
````` ::: ::: ###### Interpretation {-} - The **L10 life** of 3 904 hours means that 90% of these bearings will operate at least this long before fatigue failure. - For applications requiring **95% reliability**, use the L5 life of 2 499 hours. - At 24/7 operation, L10 represents approximately 0.4 years of service. ::: --- #### External Resources: Bearing Calculation Tools {-} Major bearing manufacturers provide comprehensive technical documentation and online calculators for bearing selection. These resources include detailed load rating tables, application examples, and life calculation methodologies. ::: {.callout-industry} **Manufacturer Resources:** - **NTN Bearing Corporation** — [Technical Calculations and Bearing Data (PDF)](https://ntn.ca/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/2203E_Web.pdf) - Comprehensive bearing catalog with life calculations, load ratings, and application guidelines - Includes worked examples for various bearing types - **NSK Ltd.** — [Rolling Bearing Catalog: Technical Section (PDF)](https://www.nsk.com/content/dam/nsk/common/catalogs/ctrgPdf/bearings/e728.pdf) - Detailed technical information on bearing selection and calculations - Includes adjusted life calculations with lubrication and contamination factors These resources are invaluable for real-world bearing selection beyond the simplified examples in this chapter. ::: --- ### Plain Bearings (Bushings) {#bushings} Plain bearings, also called **bushings** or **sleeve bearings**, are the simplest form of bearing. They consist of a bearing surface with no rolling elements—the shaft slides directly against the bearing material. ::: {.callout-think} **Before You Read:** When a shaft rotates inside a bushing, what prevents the two metal surfaces from grinding together and wearing out rapidly? Is there something more sophisticated happening than just "oil between two surfaces"? ::: #### Advantages of Bushings {-} | Advantage | Explanation | |:----------|:------------| | **Compact design** | No need for rolling elements; minimal radial space | | **Low cost** | Simple manufacturing; no precision balls or races | | **Quiet operation** | No rolling elements to generate noise | | **High load capacity** | Large contact area; excellent for shock loads | | **Self-lubricating options** | Polymer and sintered metal bushings need no external lubrication | Many of the most successful bushing designs use **sintered metals**—porous metal structures created through powder metallurgy. These porous bushings can store lubricant within their structure and release it during operation, creating truly maintenance-free bearings. ````` ::: ::: --- --- ### Hydrodynamic Lubrication and the Oil Cushion {#sec-hydrodynamic-lubrication} One of the most remarkable phenomena in bearing engineering is **hydrodynamic lubrication**—the ability of a rotating shaft to "float" on a thin cushion of oil, with complete separation between the metal surfaces. Understanding this mechanism is essential for designing reliable bushing applications. #### The Wedge Effect {#sec-wedge-effect} When a shaft begins to rotate inside a lubricated bushing, something remarkable happens. The shaft doesn't rotate concentrically within the bore—instead, it shifts slightly off-center, creating a **converging wedge** of oil between the shaft and bearing surfaces. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The hydrodynamic wedge: shaft rotation drags oil into the converging gap, building pressure that lifts the shaft.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/fig-hydrodynamic-wedge-1.png){#fig-hydrodynamic-wedge fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: The physics of this process are elegant: 1. **Shaft rotation drags oil** into the narrowing gap (viscous drag) 2. **Oil cannot escape fast enough** through the narrow exit 3. **Pressure builds up** in the converging zone 4. **The pressure "pushes back"** against the shaft, lifting it 5. **At sufficient speed**, the shaft floats entirely on oil—no metal contact This is the **hydrodynamic cushion**: a self-generated oil film that supports the shaft load through fluid pressure alone. #### The Pressure Distribution {#sec-pressure-distribution} The pressure profile that develops in the oil film is not uniform. Maximum pressure occurs in the converging wedge region, just before the minimum film thickness point: $$ p = \frac{6 \mu U}{h^2} \frac{dh}{dx} $$ {#eq-reynolds-simplified} **Where:** | Symbol | Description | |:-------|:------------| | $p$ | Local pressure in the oil film | | $\mu$ | Dynamic viscosity of the lubricant | | $U$ | Surface velocity of the shaft | | $h$ | Local film thickness | | $dh/dx$ | Rate of change of film thickness | This is a simplified form of the **Reynolds equation**, which governs hydrodynamic lubrication. The key insight is that pressure only develops where the film is **converging** ($dh/dx < 0$)—in diverging regions, the pressure drops back to ambient. ::: {.callout-industry} **Industry Application:** Modern automotive engines rely entirely on hydrodynamic lubrication for their crankshaft main bearings and connecting rod bearings. At idle speed (~800 RPM), a typical crankshaft main bearing develops oil film pressures of 5-10 MPa, supporting loads of several kilonewtons on a film just 2-5 micrometers thick. At highway speeds, this film pressure can exceed 50 MPa. ::: #### Eccentricity Ratio {#sec-eccentricity} The position of the shaft within the bearing is characterized by the **eccentricity ratio** ($\varepsilon$): $$ \varepsilon = \frac{e}{c} $$ {#eq-eccentricity-ratio} **Where:** - $e$ = distance between bearing center and shaft center (eccentricity) - $c$ = radial clearance = $(D - d)/2$ (bearing bore radius minus shaft radius) | $\varepsilon$ Value | Meaning | |:--------------------|:--------| | 0 | Shaft is perfectly centered (no load, or very high speed) | | 0.3 - 0.7 | Normal operating range for hydrodynamic bearings | | → 1.0 | Shaft approaching contact with bearing (high load or low speed) | The minimum film thickness is directly related to eccentricity: $$ h_{min} = c(1 - \varepsilon) $$ {#eq-min-film-thickness} For safe operation, the minimum film thickness must exceed the combined surface roughness of the shaft and bearing, plus a safety margin for contaminants and vibration. --- ### Oil Circulation in Sintered Bearings {#sec-oil-circulation} For sintered oil-impregnated bushings (see Chapter @sec-chap-sintering for manufacturing details), the hydrodynamic mechanism works in concert with the porous structure. The following diagram shows how oil circulates through a sintered bearing during operation: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Oil circulation mechanism in a sintered oil-impregnated bearing. The porous structure stores oil that is released during operation and recovered during rest periods.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/fig-oil-circulation-1.png){#fig-oil-circulation fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: --- ### The Stribeck Curve: Understanding Lubrication Regimes {#sec-stribeck-curve} The transition from metal-to-metal contact to full hydrodynamic separation doesn't happen instantly. German engineer Richard Stribeck (1861-1950) systematically studied this transition and developed one of the most important diagrams in tribology—the **Stribeck curve**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The Stribeck curve showing the three lubrication regimes as a function of the bearing parameter.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/fig-stribeck-curve-1.png){#fig-stribeck-curve fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: #### The Three Lubrication Regimes {#sec-lubrication-regimes} The Stribeck curve reveals three distinct operating regimes, determined by the **bearing parameter** (also called the Hersey number or Sommerfeld variable): $$ \text{Bearing Parameter} = \frac{\mu N}{P} $$ {#eq-hersey-number} **Where:** | Symbol | Description | |:-------|:------------| | $\mu$ | Dynamic viscosity of the lubricant | | $N$ | Rotational speed (or sliding velocity) | | $P$ | Bearing pressure (load per unit projected area) | --- **1. Boundary Lubrication** (Low bearing parameter) At low speeds, high loads, or low viscosity, the oil film is too thin to separate the surfaces. The shaft and bearing make direct metal-to-metal contact at their surface asperities (microscopic peaks). - **Friction coefficient:** 0.08 - 0.15 (high) - **Wear:** Significant—asperities deform and break off - **Protection:** Depends on boundary additives in the oil (anti-wear, extreme pressure) - **Typical conditions:** Startup, shutdown, slow oscillating motion ::: {.callout-check} **Quick Check:** Why is startup the most damaging period for a hydrodynamic bearing? ::: --- **2. Mixed Lubrication** (Intermediate bearing parameter) As speed increases or load decreases, a partial fluid film develops. The load is shared between the oil film (hydrodynamic pressure) and the remaining asperity contacts. - **Friction coefficient:** 0.02 - 0.08 (decreasing rapidly) - **Wear:** Moderate—some contact remains - **Transition zone:** Most sensitive to operating conditions - **Typical conditions:** Acceleration/deceleration, variable loads --- **3. Hydrodynamic Lubrication** (High bearing parameter) At sufficient speed, the shaft "lifts off" completely and floats on the oil cushion. There is no metal-to-metal contact—all load is carried by fluid pressure. - **Friction coefficient:** 0.001 - 0.01 (very low) - **Wear:** Essentially zero (only contamination-related) - **Friction source:** Viscous shearing of the oil film - **Typical conditions:** Continuous rotation at design speed Notice that friction actually **increases** slightly at very high bearing parameters. This is because the viscous drag in the oil film increases with speed—but this "friction" doesn't cause wear since no contact occurs. --- #### Practical Implications for Bearing Design {#sec-stribeck-implications} The Stribeck curve has profound implications for bearing selection and design: | Design Goal | Implication | |:------------|:------------| | **Maximize bearing life** | Operate in the hydrodynamic regime; avoid boundary conditions | | **Minimum speed requirement** | Must exceed the transition speed for hydrodynamic lubrication | | **Oil selection** | Higher viscosity → lower bearing parameter → earlier transition to hydrodynamic | | **Clearance design** | Affects film thickness and transition point | | **Startup/shutdown wear** | Unavoidable boundary contact; limit start-stop cycles or use hydrostatic assist | ::: {.callout-industry} **Industry Application:** Large turbine bearings in power plants use **hydrostatic jacking**—externally pressurized oil is pumped into the bearing at startup to lift the shaft before rotation begins. This eliminates the boundary lubrication phase entirely, preventing wear during the 10-15 seconds it takes to reach hydrodynamic speed. ::: For sintered self-lubricating bearings (see Chapter @sec-chap-sintering), the oil stored in the porous structure is released by heat and pumping action during operation. However, at very low speeds or oscillating motion, hydrodynamic films cannot develop—this is why **graphite-impregnated sintered bearings** are used instead for such applications, providing solid lubrication rather than relying on fluid film formation. --- ### Oil Circulation in Sintered Bearings (continued) {#sec-oil-circulation-diagram} The following diagram illustrates how oil circulates through a sintered oil-impregnated bearing during operation. The porous structure acts as an oil reservoir, continuously replenishing the hydrodynamic film: ### PV Limits for Bushings {#pv-limits} The **PV limit** is the most important design criterion for plain bearings. It represents the maximum combination of **bearing pressure** (P) and **sliding velocity** (V) that the bearing material can sustain without excessive wear or failure. #### The PV Concept {-} $$PV = P \times V$$ **Where:** | Symbol | Description | Typical Units | |:-------|:------------|:--------------| | $P$ | Bearing pressure | psi (or MPa) | | $V$ | Sliding velocity | ft/min (or m/s) | | $PV$ | PV factor | psi·ft/min (or MPa·m/s) | #### Calculating Bearing Pressure (P) {-} For a journal bearing (shaft in a bushing): $$P = \frac{F}{d \times L}$$ **Where:** | Symbol | Description | |:-------|:------------| | $F$ | Radial load on the bearing (lbf or N) | | $d$ | Shaft (journal) diameter (in or mm) | | $L$ | Bearing length (in or mm) | > **Note:** This is the **projected area** method, using $A = d \times L$, not the cylindrical surface area. #### Calculating Sliding Velocity (V) {-} $$V = \pi \times d \times n$$ For consistent units: **English:** $$V = \frac{\pi \times d \times n}{12} \quad \text{(ft/min, where } d \text{ in inches, } n \text{ in RPM)}$$ **Metric:** $$V = \frac{\pi \times d \times n}{60,000} \quad \text{(m/s, where } d \text{ in mm, } n \text{ in RPM)}$$ --- #### PV Limit Visualization {-} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![PV limit diagram showing safe operating region for different bushing materials.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/pv-limit-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: --- #### Design Rules for PV {-} 1. **Calculate the actual PV** for your application 2. **Select a bushing material** with a PV limit **at least 2× higher** than calculated 3. **Check individual P and V limits** separately (materials have maximums for each) 4. **Consider temperature effects**—PV limits decrease at elevated temperatures ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

The shaft diameter is **1.5 inches** and the bushing length is **2.0 inches**. The radial load on the bushing is **800 lbf**. Determine: 1. The bearing pressure ($P$) 2. The sliding velocity ($V$) 3. The PV value 4. Whether a SAE 660 bronze bushing is suitable ::: ::: {.answer} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Step Formula Calculation Result
Step 1: Bearing Pressure P = F / (d × L) P = 800 / (1.5 × 2) 266.7 psi
Step 2: Sliding Velocity V = π·d·n / 12 V = π × 1.5 × 500 / 12 196.3 ft/min
Step 3: PV Factor PV = P × V PV = 266.7 × 196.3 52 360 psi·ft/min
Step 4: Check P Limit P < P_max (4,000 psi) 266.7 < 4,000? OK ✓

The shaft has a diameter of **5/16 in**. The self-lubricating bushing is made of **Bronze-Iron**. The bushing has a length of **0.5 in**. What is the **maximum speed** (in RPM) the motor is allowed to spin? ::: ::: {.answer} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Maximum Speed Calculation Steps
Step Formula Calculation Result
Step 1: Bearing Pressure P = F / (d × L) P = 20 / (0.3125 × 0.5) 128 psi
Step 2: Check P < P_max P < 2,500 psi? 128 < 2,500? OK ✓
Step 3: Max V from V limit V_max = 800 ft/min V ≤ 800 800 ft/min
Step 4: Max V from PV limit V = PV_max / P V = 35,000 / 128 273.4 ft/min
Step 5: N from V limit N = 12·V / (π·d) N = 12 × 800 / (π × 0.3125) 9 778 RPM
Step 6: N from PV limit N = 12·V / (π·d) N = 12 × 273.4 / (π × 0.3125) 3 342 RPM
Step 7: Governing Limit N_max = min(N_V, N_PV) min(9 778, 3 342) 3 342 RPM
````` ::: ::: ###### Conclusion {-} The **PV limit governs** this design. Although the V limit alone would allow 9 778 RPM, the combined PV constraint limits the speed to: $$N_{max} = \boxed{3 342\ \text{RPM}}$$ ::: {.callout-think} **Why does the PV limit govern?** The bearing pressure (P = 128 psi) is low compared to the 2,500 psi maximum, but when multiplied by velocity, it quickly approaches the PV limit. This is a common scenario with small-diameter, lightly-loaded bushings operating at high speeds. ::: ::: --- ### Applied Example: Minimum Bushing Length {#bushing-example-length} ::: {.question} A bushing is loaded with **20 lbf**. The minimum bushing length is: $$L_{min} = \boxed{0.52\ \text{in}}$$ In practice, you would round up to the next standard size (e.g., **0.5625 in = 9/16 in** or **0.625 in = 5/8 in**) to provide a safety margin. ::: --- ### Applied Example: Maximum Load Capacity {#bushing-example-load} ::: {.question} A shaft runs at **3,500 RPM** and has a diameter of **5/16 in**. The self-lubricating bushing is made of **Bronze-Iron** and has a length of **0.5 in**. What is the **maximum load** (in lbf) the bushing can handle? ::: ::: {.answer} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Maximum Load Calculation Steps
Step Formula Calculation Result
Step 1: Sliding Velocity V = π·d·n / 12 V = π × 0.3125 × 3500 / 12 286.3 ft/min
Step 2: Check V < V_max V < 800 ft/min? 286.3 < 800? OK ✓

Step 4: Max P from PV limit P_max = PV_max / V P_max = 35,000 / 286.3 122.2 psi

The maximum allowable load is: $$F_{max} = \boxed{19.1\ \text{lbf}}$$ ::: {.callout-industry} **Design Insight:** Notice that at 3,500 RPM with a 0.5 in bushing, the maximum load is only about 19 lbf—very close to the 20 lbf used in the previous examples. This illustrates why it's critical to check both P/V limits AND the combined PV limit. The individual limits (P < 2,500 psi, V < 800 ft/min) are both easily satisfied, but the PV combination becomes the controlling factor at higher speeds. If your application requires 20 lbf at 3,500 RPM, you would need to either: 1. Increase the bushing length (as calculated in the previous example: L ≥ 0.52 in) 2. Select a material with a higher PV limit (e.g., SAE 660 Bronze with PV = 75,000) ::: ::: --- ### Bearing vs. Bushing Selection Guide {#sec-selection-guide} When should you use a ball bearing versus a bushing? The choice depends on operating conditions, space constraints, and maintenance requirements. For bushings, the decision between oil-impregnated and solid-lubricant types depends on the motion profile and environment—continuous rotation favors oil-impregnated bearings that can develop hydrodynamic films, while oscillating or high-temperature applications favor graphite-impregnated designs (see Chapter @sec-chap-sintering for details on manufacturing both types). See Chapter @sec-chap-sintering for details on how porosity is controlled during manufacturing to optimize oil storage capacity. --- ### Design Checklist {-} **For Ball Bearings:** - [ ] Determine radial and axial loads - [ ] Calculate equivalent dynamic load ($P$) - [ ] Select bearing with $C/P$ ratio giving adequate life - [ ] Verify speed is below limiting speed - [ ] Apply reliability and operating condition factors if needed - [ ] Specify lubrication and sealing requirements **For Bushings:** - [ ] Calculate bearing pressure ($P$) - [ ] Calculate sliding velocity ($V$) - [ ] Verify $P < P_{max}$ for selected material - [ ] Verify $V < V_{max}$ for selected material - [ ] Verify $PV < PV_{limit}$ with safety factor ≥ 2 - [ ] Consider temperature effects on PV limits - [ ] Specify lubrication (if required) or confirm dry-running capability **For Hydrodynamic Lubrication (Oil-Impregnated Bushings):** - [ ] Verify minimum operating speed exceeds transition to hydrodynamic regime - [ ] Calculate bearing parameter ($\mu N / P$) and confirm operation in hydrodynamic zone - [ ] Estimate minimum film thickness and compare to surface roughness - [ ] For sintered bearings: verify porosity level (20-30%) for adequate oil storage—see Chapter @sec-chap-sintering - [ ] Consider startup/shutdown wear; limit start-stop cycles or use hydrostatic jacking - [ ] Select oil viscosity appropriate for operating temperature range **For Solid-Lubricant Bushings (Graphite/MoS₂):** - [ ] Confirm motion type: oscillating, reciprocating, or slow rotation (hydrodynamic not feasible) - [ ] Verify temperature requirements (graphite to 500°C, MoS₂ to 400°C) - [ ] Check environmental requirements (vacuum, contamination, food-safe) - [ ] See Chapter @sec-chap-sintering for graphite impregnation specifications
